newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada tobacco makers to comply with new law.
newsitem.headline: Canada tobacco makers to comply with new law.

text.p: Canadian tobacco makers said Tuesday that they would comply with a new federal law limiting tobacco advertising, after failing to get a court order blocking the measure.

Michel Descoteaux, a spokesman for Montreal-based Imasco Ltd. unit Imperial Tobacco, Canada's largest cigarette maker, told Reuters that the company was moving quickly to remove tobacco advertising from all retail outlets across Canada.
"We have already begun and are continuing as fast as we can," Descoteaux said.
Canada's third largest tobacco maker, RJR-MacDonald, which is wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International, also said it would comply with the new law.
Quebec Superior Court Justice Danielle Grenier Tuesday refused the tobacco companies' request for an injunction blocking the law.
But the tobacco makers said they would continue their court challenge of the law on constitutional grounds, arguing that it unfairly restricted their freedom of expression.
Canada's Tobacco Act became law on April 25. It restricts tobacco advertising and bans vending machine sales of tobacco. It also restricts tobacco company sponsorship of sporting and cultural events.

"Although we support the need for reasonable restrictions on tobacco marketing practices and the government's objective of preventing youth smoking, we believe the new Tobacco Act is simply unconstitutional," RJR-Macdonald Chief Executive Richard Kauffeld said in a statement.
Kauffeld said the new law disregarded a Canadian Supreme Court ruling that struck down a similar law, the Tobacco Products Control Act, in September 1995.
He said the removal of tobacco product advertising materials from more than 40,000 retail outlets and outdoor advertising across Canada was an enormous task.
The anti-tobacco law has also provoked soul-searching by arts and sporting groups across Canada that receive funding from the tobacco companies.

Organisations in charge of the Montreal International Jazz Festival, the Grand Prix of Montreal formula one car race and car races in Toronto and Vancouver have criticised the law for plunging them into funding crises.
Imasco is 40 percent-owned by B.A.T Industries Plc of Britain.
